messages.subject: Interpreting reading time data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I conducted a self-paced reading experiment and would like some advice on
interpreting the analysis results.

The research question was if definite and indefinite NPs would take
different reading times when they were given in the contexts where either
unique or non-unique referents are presupposed. (articles x contexts; 2x2
design; latin-squared)

The hypothesis was that when the (in)definiteness of an NP and the
(non-)uniqueness of its referent are matched (definite/unique;
indefinite/non-unique), the reading time will be significantly faster than
when they were unmatched (definite/non-unique; indefinite/unique). The log
RT pattern shows roughly the predicted pattern.



  *
                    *
*                   *
          *         *                                           *
*         *
*         *         *        *                       *         *
*         *
*         *         *        *                       *         *
*         *
d-u     d-n     i-u     i-n                    d-u     d-n     i-u     i-n

log RT                                            log RT residuals

where

d-u means definite article in unique referent context (match)
d-i means  definite article in non-unique referent context (mismatch)
i-u means indefinite article in unique referent context (mismatch)
i-n means indefinite article in non-unique referent context (match)

The log RT analysis shows the predicted pattern. That is, mismatch
conditions show longer RTs and there is a marginally significant
interaction of article x context. But the residual analysis shows a main
effect of context (much longer RT in non-unique referent contexts), a main
effect of article (longer RT in indefinite condition), and an interaction
effect of article and context.

I need help in interpreting the residual analysis results.

Thank you,
Hannah

characters.  However, there are also other ways to residualize that

messages.subject: How to draw lessons from a possibly overpowered study?
messages.subject_clean: How to draw lessons from a possibly overpowered study?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

Last year I carried out an experiment that I plan to elaborate on in the 
months to come. I think, however, that the first experiment was 
*overpowered – *I may have recruited more participants than necessary to 
get a decent power level. This may be a strange thing to say but 
participants (and the means to reimburse them) are at a premium so I’d 
rather not recruite 80 participants where 30 will do. I’ve tried to run 
some simulations to figure out how much power I would’ve had, had I 
recruited fewer participants, but I’m not sure whether they make any 
sense. The goal is to get an estimate of how many participants I should 
recruit for the next experiment without wasting resources.


*The experiment*

The set-up of the experiment was as follows. Participants are randomly 
assigned to one of two learning conditions, each serving as the other’s 
control group. All (German-speaking) participants are shown Dutch words 
that have German cognates. In one condition, some of these are words 
spelt with <oe>, which correspond to German words with <u>. In the other 
condition, some of the words are spelt with <ij>, which correspond to 
German words with <ei>. In the testing phase, all participants are shown 
the same words (a mixture of Dutch words with <oe>, with <ij> and 
fillers) so see whether participants in the <oe> learning condition are 
more likely to translate words with <oe> by German words with <u> and 
participants in the <ij> condition words with <ij> by German words with 
<ei> than their respective controls (binary dependent variable). I 
recruited 80 participants; each participant provided translations for 21 
<oe> and 21 <ij> words.

A shortened version of the dataset is available from 
http://homeweb.unifr.ch/VanhoveJ/Pub/Data/dat_post_critical.csv.

*Results*

The interaction between LearningCondition and stimulus Category (oe or 
ij word) was pretty large (1.9 +/- 0.3 log-odds), which made me think 
that 80 participants may have been overkill for this design.

###
dat_post_critical <- 
read.csv("http://homeweb.unifr.ch/VanhoveJ/Pub/Data/dat_post_critical.csv")

mod0 <- glmer(CorrectVowel ~ LearningCondition + Category + (1 + 
Category | Subject) + (1 + LearningCondition | Item),data = 
dat_post_critical, family = binomial,control = 
glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"))

mod1 <- update(mod0, . ~ . + LearningCondition:Category)

anova(mod0, mod1)

###

*A simulation of sorts*

I randomly restrict the dataset to ‘n’ participants, divided evenly 
between the conditions and then run the same analysis as above on this 
restricted dataset. I do this, say, 100 times for the ‘n’ that I’m 
interested in and see how many analyses return a significant 
interaction. This probably isn’t entirely kosher, but might it 
nonetheless serve as a ballpark guideline for a future experiment?

###

power.simulation <- function(n) {

# Randomly 'recruit' n/2 participants from the ij learning condition

dat1 <- subset(dat_post_critical, Subject %in% 
sample(unique(dat_post_critical[dat_post_critical$LearningCondition == 
"<ij> participants",]$Subject), size = n/2))

# 'Recruit' n/2 participants from the oe learning condition

dat2 <- subset(dat_post_critical, Subject %in% 
sample(unique(dat_post_critical[dat_post_critical$LearningCondition == 
"<oe> participants",]$Subject), size = n/2))

# Combine datasets

dat <- droplevels(rbind(dat1, dat2))

# Carry out model comparison on reduced dataset

mod0 <- glmer(CorrectVowel ~ LearningCondition + Category + (1 + 
Category | Subject) + (1 + LearningCondition | Item), data = dat, family 
= binomial, control = glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"))

mod1 <- update(mod0, . ~ . + LearningCondition:Category)

# Save p-value for interaction

pvalue <- anova(mod0, mod1)[2, 8]

return(pvalue)

}


# Simulate 100 runs for n = 16 (8 in each condition)

# This takes a while, hence only 100 runs.

ps.n16 <- replicate(100, power.simulation(n = 16))


table(ps.n16 < 0.05)

# 80 = TRUE


# For n = 30 (15 per condition), I got 99 TRUE


###


Is it okay to conclude that I might as well have recruited only 30ish 
instead of 80 participants? (Which would be a useful thing to know for 
next time.)


Thanks,
Jan


-- 

Jan Vanhove, Department of Multilingualism, University of Fribourg, 
Switzerland

messages.subject: Re: How to draw lessons from a possibly overpowered study?
messages.subject_clean: How to draw lessons from a possibly overpowered study?
messages.body_plain:
This is really nice, Jan!

I think the catch is that this inherits the problem with post hoc power
analyses in that they basically just recapitulate p-values in some way.

Here's the intuition: one of the well-known problems with *under*powered
studies is that if they happen to find a significant effect, then that
effect is almost certainly overestimated. So the trap here is that it's
possible that "in truth" (i.e., in the larger population beyond your 80
participants) the effect you are looking for (the interaction) is much
smaller,and you just got "lucky" and found a much bigger effect than
normal. Your approach here will basically then estimate power assuming the
current effect estimate is in fact the true effect size. If that's an
overestimate, then your power conclusions will be overly optimistic as
well.  To put it another way, a very small p-value and a large effect may
not indicate that this is an overpowered study with 80. It is also
consistent with the study being *under*powered (and lucky)!

A more conservative approach would be to simulate a smaller effect size,
and then do what you did in terms of running a bunch of simulated "studies"
to see what N you need to consistently return TRUE on your test.  So,
instead of checking the ability to find an effect of 1.9, look to see if
you can find an effect of 1.3 (which is minus 2 std errs) or even 1.0 (the
size of the other effects) or smaller.

Hope this helps,
-scott

> – *I may have recruited more participants than necessary to get a decent
> power level. This may be a strange thing to say but participants (and the
> means to reimburse them) are at a premium so I’d rather not recruite 80
> participants where 30 will do. I’ve tried to run some simulations to
> figure out how much power I would’ve had, had I recruited fewer
> participants, but I’m not sure whether they make any sense. The goal is to
> get an estimate of how many participants I should recruit for the next
> experiment without wasting resources.
>
>
> *The experiment*
>
> The set-up of the experiment was as follows. Participants are randomly
> assigned to one of two learning conditions, each serving as the other’s
> control group. All (German-speaking) participants are shown Dutch words
> that have German cognates. In one condition, some of these are words spelt
> with <oe>, which correspond to German words with <u>. In the other
> condition, some of the words are spelt with <ij>, which correspond to
> German words with <ei>. In the testing phase, all participants are shown
> the same words (a mixture of Dutch words with <oe>, with <ij> and fillers)
> so see whether participants in the <oe> learning condition are more likely
> to translate words with <oe> by German words with <u> and participants in
> the <ij> condition words with <ij> by German words with <ei> than their
> respective controls (binary dependent variable). I recruited 80
> participants; each participant provided translations for 21 <oe> and 21
> <ij> words.
>
> A shortened version of the dataset is available from
> http://homeweb.unifr.ch/VanhoveJ/Pub/Data/dat_post_critical.csv.
>
> *Results*
>
> The interaction between LearningCondition and stimulus Category (oe or ij
> word) was pretty large (1.9 +/- 0.3 log-odds), which made me think that 80
> participants may have been overkill for this design.
>
> ###
> dat_post_critical <- read.csv("
> http://homeweb.unifr.ch/VanhoveJ/Pub/Data/dat_post_critical.csv")
>
> mod0 <- glmer(CorrectVowel ~ LearningCondition + Category + (1 + Category
> | Subject) + (1 + LearningCondition | Item), data = dat_post_critical,
> family = binomial, control = glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"))
>
> mod1 <- update(mod0, . ~ . + LearningCondition:Category)
>
> anova(mod0, mod1)
>
> ###
>
>  *A simulation of sorts*
>
> I randomly restrict the dataset to ‘n’ participants, divided evenly
> between the conditions and then run the same analysis as above on this
> restricted dataset. I do this, say, 100 times for the ‘n’ that I’m
> interested in and see how many analyses return a significant interaction.
> This probably isn’t entirely kosher, but might it nonetheless serve as a
> ballpark guideline for a future experiment?
>
> ###
>
> power.simulation <- function(n) {
>
> # Randomly 'recruit' n/2 participants from the ij learning condition
>
> dat1 <- subset(dat_post_critical, Subject %in%
> sample(unique(dat_post_critical[dat_post_critical$LearningCondition ==
> "<ij> participants",]$Subject), size = n/2))
>
>   # 'Recruit' n/2 participants from the oe learning condition
>
> dat2 <- subset(dat_post_critical, Subject %in%
> sample(unique(dat_post_critical[dat_post_critical$LearningCondition ==
> "<oe> participants",]$Subject), size = n/2))
>
>   # Combine datasets
>
> dat <- droplevels(rbind(dat1, dat2))
>
>   # Carry out model comparison on reduced dataset
>
> mod0 <- glmer(CorrectVowel ~ LearningCondition + Category + (1 + Category
> | Subject) + (1 + LearningCondition | Item), data = dat, family = binomial,
> control = glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"))
>
> mod1 <- update(mod0, . ~ . + LearningCondition:Category)
>
>   # Save p-value for interaction
>
> pvalue <- anova(mod0, mod1)[2, 8]
>
> return(pvalue)
>
> }
>
>
>  # Simulate 100 runs for n = 16 (8 in each condition)
>
> # This takes a while, hence only 100 runs.
>
> ps.n16 <- replicate(100, power.simulation(n = 16))
>
>
>  table(ps.n16 < 0.05)
>
> # 80 = TRUE
>
>
>  # For n = 30 (15 per condition), I got 99 TRUE
>
>
>  ###
>
>
>  Is it okay to conclude that I might as well have recruited only 30ish
> instead of 80 participants? (Which would be a useful thing to know for next
> time.)
>
>
> Thanks,
> Jan
>
>
>  --
>
> Jan Vanhove, Department of Multilingualism, University of Fribourg,
> Switzerland
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Scott. Do you mean something like this?

###
# Fit model
mod <- glmer(CorrectVowel ~ LearningCondition + Category + 
LearningCondition:Category + (1 + Category | Subject) + (1 + 
LearningCondition | Item), data = dat_post_critical, family = binomial, 
control = glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"))

# Get RE estimates ('relative Cholesky factors of each RE term', so I 
learn. Not that that rings a bell.)
thetas <- getME(mod,"theta")

# Get FE estimates
betas <- fixef(mod)
# and change the 1.92 for the interaction to 1.27
betas[4] <- 1.9292 - 2*0.3292

# Function for simulating new data
power.simulation2 <- function(n) {

   # Generate new data
   dat_post_critical$New <- factor(unlist(simulate(mod, newparams = 
list(theta = thetas, beta = betas))))

   # And randomly reduce this dataset (as before)
   dat1 <- subset(dat_post_critical,
                  Subject %in% 
sample(unique(dat_post_critical[dat_post_critical$LearningCondition == 
"<ij> participants",]$Subject), size = n/2))
   dat2 <- subset(dat_post_critical,
                  Subject %in% 
sample(unique(dat_post_critical[dat_post_critical$LearningCondition == 
"<oe> participants",]$Subject), size = n/2))
   dat <- droplevels(rbind(dat1, dat2))

   # Run new model comparison
   mod0 <- glmer(New ~ LearningCondition + Category + (1 + Category | 
Subject) + (1 + LearningCondition | Item), data = dat, family = 
binomial, control = glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"))
   mod1 <- update(mod0, . ~ . + LearningCondition:Category)

   # Save and return p-value
   pvalue <- anova(mod0, mod1)[2, 8]
   return(pvalue)
}

# Run 100 times for 40 participants
ps.n40b <- replicate(100, power.simulation2(n = 40))

table(ps.n40b < 0.05)
# 82% TRUE
###

But then don't I have the same problem as before, i.e. that I assume 
that my estimation of the random effect variability also holds for the 
next study?

(Incidentally, I've been thinking about how the inclusion of covariates 
that are pretty easy to collect and have consistently been shown to 
explain between-item and between-participant variance that I'm not 
really interested in here would contribute to the study's power. But the 
literature on covariate adjustment in logistic models is a bit too 
complicated for me at the moment.)

Cheers,
Jan
-- 

Jan Vanhove, Department of Multilingualism, University of Fribourg, 
Switzerland

genuine research questions

messages.body_plain:
Nice!  Yep, that's exactly the kind of thing I had in mind.

And sure, any of the parameters in your model, including the other effects
and random effect variances, could be quite different in "reality" (i.e.,
the larger population) from what you observed.  And so you could run some
more alternatives checking some different sets of assumptions.  But I think
given this current example, the thing to worry most about is the
possibility that the effect size of 1.9 from your 80-person study could be
an overestimate, so I think what you've done here is a very reasonable
step. In other words, I think the particular assumption that the effect you
care about (the interaction) is accurate is the most dangerous for the
purposes of estimating N sizes for power, so playing with that one, exactly
as you've done here, is a really useful step.

In terms of the covariate thing, I say just keep playing with some
simulations, and that'll probably be more immediately helpful than the
literature :-)

best,
-scott
